name: Gum recession treatment
lead: Gum recession treatment refers to the procedures used to restore or cover gum that has pulled back from the teeth and exposed the roots. Recession is common: one meta-analysis cited in encyclopedic sources estimates that about 85 percent of people worldwide have it on at least one tooth, and a 2026 study puts the figure at roughly 81 percent.[1][3] Periodontal disease is its most common cause.[1]

Options include pedicle grafts, free gingival and connective tissue grafts, acellular dermal matrix, and growth-factor techniques; healing takes about two to four weeks.[1] Studies and registered trials compare grafts with collagen membranes, platelet-rich fibrin, placental membrane and other techniques.[4][5][6][7]
infobox: Pedicle graft, free gingival graft, connective tissue graft, dermal matrix

paras: Periodontal disease is the most common cause. Other reported causes include aggressive brushing, thin gum tissue, tobacco, trauma, crowded teeth and piercings; evidence linking brushing to recession is described as inconclusive.[1]

A periodontist can regenerate gum tissue using nearby tissue, palatal grafts or a donor dermal matrix, usually under local anaesthesia. Growth-factor-infused bone graft material is another option described.[1] Complete or near-complete coverage is described as possible when there is no periodontal bone loss, though that statement is marked as needing citation.[1] A trial of Russian origin examined autogenous oral mucosa fibroblast injections, reporting increased gum thickness and reduced recession for at least nine months.[2]

Registered trials compare a xenogenic collagen membrane with connective tissue graft,[4] platelet-rich fibrin with connective tissue graft and coronally advanced flap alone,[7] coronally advanced flap with or without PRF,[5] placental membrane for root coverage,[6] de-epithelialised free gingival graft[8] and cyanoacrylate adhesive versus suture.[9] Results are not summarised here.
A 2026 cross-sectional analysis evaluated the reliability and educational value of YouTube videos on gingival recession and its management.[3]

card.summary: The family of gum surgeries, mostly grafts, aimed at covering exposed roots; widely studied, outcomes vary by technique.
card.note: Healing takes weeks; results depend on technique and bone support.

quick.overview:
Gum recession treatment covers procedures that cover exposed roots and rebuild the gum line, mainly gum grafts taken from the palate or a donor matrix, plus flap techniques and growth-factor products.

Recession is very common, and many registered trials compare techniques, though the sources reviewed give few outcome figures.
quick.mechanism: Tissue is moved, grafted or regenerated over the exposed root surface and sutured or secured while it heals over about two to four weeks.
quick.risks: Encyclopedic sources reviewed do not detail risks. Cause matters: periodontal disease, tooth position and brushing habits are among those cited, and treatment of the cause is separate from covering the recession.
